newsitem.title: USA: Tuskegee study's legacy is mistrust among blacks.
newsitem.headline: Tuskegee study's legacy is mistrust among blacks.

text.p: A quarter-century after a U.S. government experiment left hundreds of black men to suffer syphilis without treatment, a legacy of mistrust of the health care establishment lingers among African-Americans.

"I think there's a continuing mistrust, and I think there are things continuing today that perpetuate it," said Dr. Lovell Jones, a professor at the University of Texas in Houston and a longtime advocate for minority health care.

Conducted by the U.S. Public Health Service in Macon County, Alabama between 1932 and 1972, the so-called Tuskegee study charted the progress of untreated syphilis among 399 poor black men, most of them sharecroppers or day labourers.

As President Bill Clinton apologised on Friday to the eight surviving subjects of the experiment, Jones and others in and out of the American black community decried the climate of scepticism that can leave minorities on the sidelines of medical research and treatment.

Jones said the federal medical bureaucracy can be creaky when it comes to including blacks in clinical trials of new techniques and drugs, and that black physicians and researchers need to be encouraged to participate in the process.

"I think that there's a lack of sensitivity that probably goes all the way up the chain," Jones said in a telephone interview. "I get the sense that at least in certain segments of society, lives aren't valued. The Tuskegee thing is just one event in a whole series of events."
Clinton recognised the continued need for remedies to the mindset that allowed the Tuskegee experiment to go forward.

"The legacy of the study at Tuskegee has reached far and deep in ways that hurt our progress and divide our nation," Clinton said in a White House ceremony. "We cannot be one America when a whole segment of our nation has no trust in America. An apology is the first step, and we take it with a commitment to rebuild that broken trust."
Clinton outlined improvements planned to shore up trust, including increased community involvement in health care, and better grounding for medical researchers in bioethics.

Officials at the Department of Health and Human Services acknowledged the gap between whites and blacks in research and treatment, and aimed to narrow it through offering more fellowships for black researchers, and a new curriculum for all medical professionals.

The Journal of the National Medical Association, the oldest U.S. organisation of African-American physicians, reported last year that in addition to being under-represented in clinical trials, blacks have "a general lack of access to care and use of preventive and palliative medical diagnostic and treatment services."
The association's president, Dr. Randall Morgan, said Clinton's apology would go a long way to convincing blacks that participation in clinical trials would benefit them.
Another key to healing is the increased involvement of black doctors, Morgan said in a telephone interview.
"African-American physicians take care of African-American patients, and if those physicians are involved so will their patients be involved and that really is the key," Morgan said.
Sen. Carol Moseley-Braun, an Illinois Democrat applauded the Clinton apology, but said the lessons of Tuskegee may not have been absorbed.

Moseley Braun said government-sponsored studies on the effectiveness of the drug AZT in preventing transmission of the AIDS virus from mothers to children still give some mothers a placebo, even though AZT has been shown to be effective for this purpose.

"We must never allow unknowing patients to be abused as they were in the Tuskegee scandal, and we must not put people in harm's way in the name of science when there is clearly no rational excuse to take such risks,' she said in a statement.
